lead: FM reception has a hidden problem: after the discriminator, noise power grows with audio frequency, so the treble sounds hissy. Pre-emphasis boosts the treble in the transmitter before modulation; de-emphasis cuts the treble in the receiver after detection. The voice or music returns to normal, but the high-frequency noise is cut too. Broadcast FM in the Americas uses a 75 µs time constant; Europe, India and most of the world use 50 µs. The idea is used in FM radio, TV sound and wireless microphones.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.5 for the noise triangle and figure of merit, and Chapter 3.4 for the discriminator output.

blocks.text: The input noise at an FM receiver is white: its power spectral density is flat across the RF band. The discriminator does not keep it flat. It converts a frequency offset into a voltage, so a noise component that sits f hertz away from the carrier produces an output voltage proportional to f. Power is proportional to the square of voltage. The output noise power spectral density therefore rises as f² across the audio band. Plotted against audio frequency, the amplitude spectrum is a triangle and the power spectrum is a parabola. Engineers call it the noise triangle.

Speech and music do not have equal power at all audio frequencies. Most energy is at low and middle frequencies; high notes and consonants are weaker. At 10 kHz the signal may be 20 dB below its low-frequency level while the noise is much higher. The treble signal-to-noise ratio is poor even when the overall SNR looks good.

Pre-emphasis fixes this before transmission. The transmitter passes the audio through a network that boosts high frequencies. The receiver passes the discriminator output through the inverse network. The signal is boosted then cut back, so it ends where it started. The noise is not boosted at the transmitter. At the receiver it is cut along with the treble. The net effect is a large SNR gain at high frequencies.
One condition: the boost must be modest and the deviation must be set after the pre-emphasis network, because boosting treble raises the peak audio voltage and with it the FM deviation.
The pre-emphasis response is a first-order boost. A resistor and capacitor set the time constant τ = RC, where R is resistance in ohms and C is capacitance in farads.

blocks.where: H_pre(f) is the voltage gain at audio frequency f (Hz); f1 is the corner frequency (Hz); τ = RC is the time constant in seconds.

blocks.text: Below f1 the gain is about 1. Above f1 the gain rises at 6 dB per octave. De-emphasis is the mirror image.

blocks.where: H_de(f) is the de-emphasis voltage gain; the same f1 is used at both ends, so the two responses multiply to 1 at every frequency.

blocks.text: With de-emphasis, the high-frequency noise is reduced. For an audio band extending to fm, with fm much greater than f1, the output SNR improvement is approximately:

blocks.where: fm is the highest audio frequency in Hz; f1 is the corner frequency; the result is a power ratio when fm is much greater than f1.

blocks.text: The American 75 µs system with fm = 15 kHz gives f1 = 2122 Hz, ratio 7.07, improvement about 16.7, or 12.2 dB. The formula counts the reduction of the parabolic noise. It does not apply when fm is close to f1.

Put pre-emphasis in the audio path before the FM modulator. Put de-emphasis after the FM discriminator, before the audio power amplifier. The transmitter network must see the microphone or line signal, not the modulated carrier. The receiver network must see the recovered audio, not the IF signal.

Time constants must match at the two ends. A 75 µs transmitter needs a 75 µs receiver. If the receiver uses 50 µs, the treble is cut too little, so the sound is bright and noisy. If the transmitter uses 50 µs and the receiver 75 µs, the treble is cut too much and the sound is dull.

In a broadcast chain the pre-emphasis is inside the exciter. The receiver chip or software-defined radio applies de-emphasis after the discriminator. In a stereo receiver the de-emphasis is placed after the stereo decoder, so it acts on the recovered left and right channels. Placing it before the decoder would cut the L+R baseband and the L−R subcarrier by different amounts and spoil the stereo separation; that decoder is the subject of Chapter 3.8.

figure.caption: The pre-emphasis gain rises above 2122 Hz; the de-emphasis gain falls by the same factor, so the two curves multiply to one flat line.

spec.aria: The boost curve rises with frequency at 6 dB per octave and the cut curve is its exact inverse, so their product is flat across the audio band.

examples.question: An American broadcast FM system uses a 75 µs pre-emphasis. Find the corner frequency, the voltage boost at 2.122 kHz and at 15 kHz in dB, and estimate the SNR improvement for a 15 kHz audio band in ratio and dB.
steps: At f = 2122 Hz, f/f1 = 1. Gain = √(1 + 1²) = √2 = 1.414. Boost in dB = 20 log₁₀ 1.414 = 3.01 dB.
SNR improvement ratio = (1/3)(fm/f1)² = (1/3)(7.07)² = 16.7. In dB = 10 log₁₀ 16.7 = 12.2 dB.
examples.answer: f1 = 2122 Hz; boost = 3.01 dB at 2.122 kHz and 17.1 dB at 15 kHz; SNR improvement ≈ 16.7, that is 12.2 dB.
examples.check:
import math
tau = 75e-6
f1 = 1/(2*math.pi*tau)
g1 = math.sqrt(1 + (2122/f1)**2)
db1 = 20*math.log10(g1)
g2 = math.sqrt(1 + (15000/f1)**2)
db2 = 20*math.log10(g2)
imp = (1/3)*(15000/f1)**2
imp_db = 10*math.log10(imp)
print(round(f1))
print(round(db1, 2))
print(round(g2, 2))
print(round(db2, 1))
print(round(imp, 1))
print(round(imp_db, 1))

traps: Swapping the two networks puts the treble boost at the receiver, so the noise triangle is boosted instead of cut; the signal shape is still restored but the SNR at high frequencies gets roughly 12 dB worse instead of better. Pre-emphasis belongs at the transmitter, de-emphasis at the receiver.
Using 10 log instead of 20 log for a voltage gain gives half the correct boost in dB.
Forgetting to convert microseconds to seconds in f1 = 1/(2πτ) puts the corner out by a factor of 10⁶.
The improvement (1/3)(fm/f1)² is a power ratio; quote 10 log₁₀ of it in dB, not 20 log₁₀.
Pre-emphasis does not remove the noise triangle; it reshapes the signal before transmission so de-emphasis can cut the noise afterward.

quiz.q: What is pre-emphasis and where is it placed?
quiz.a: A high-frequency boost in the audio path before the FM modulator.

quiz.q: Why does discriminator output noise power rise as f²?
quiz.a: The discriminator converts frequency offset to voltage, so noise voltage is proportional to f and noise power to f².

quiz.q: A 50 µs system is used. Find f1 and the voltage gain at 10 kHz in dB.
For the American 75 µs system and fm = 15 kHz, estimate the SNR improvement ratio and dB.
Why must de-emphasis follow the discriminator, not precede it?
quiz.a: Before the detector it would cut signal treble and RF noise together and give no noise-triangle advantage. After the discriminator it cuts the already-shaped audio noise.

quiz.q: Why does pre-emphasis slightly raise FM deviation?
quiz.a: The treble boost raises the peak audio voltage, so the modulator produces a larger peak frequency swing unless deviation is reset.

quiz.q: What is the product of the pre-emphasis and de-emphasis responses?
quiz.a: One at every frequency, so the audio spectrum is restored.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same trick appears in digital audio as pre-emphasis flags in older PCM formats and in some optical recording standards. Software-defined FM receivers implement de-emphasis as a one-pole IIR filter after the discriminator. Search terms: FM pre-emphasis time constant, de-emphasis filter, 75 µs, 50 µs, discriminator noise triangle.
